headline: Operator RegExp patterns are matched against the whole value: form validation and CORS origins
summary: Two places matched an operator-supplied RegExp with an unanchored `.test()`, where a whole-string match was expected. `b.forms.validate` tested a field's `pattern` unanchored, so a value that merely contained a match passed server-side even though the browser rejects it: the same pattern is rendered as the HTML5 `pattern=` attribute, which the browser anchors over the entire value, so `pattern: /[0-9]{4}/` accepted `"12345"` (and `/[a-z]{3}/` accepted `"abc; DROP TABLE users"`) on the server while the client refused them. Server-side validation now anchors the pattern to the whole value (`^(?:source)$`, preserving flags), matching the browser and closing the client/server divergence. Separately, `b.middleware.cors` screened RegExp origins for ReDoS but not for anchoring, so an unanchored pattern like `/example\.com/` with `credentials:true` reflected `https://example.com.attacker.test` into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` (a credential-reflection bypass); `create()` now refuses a RegExp origin that is not anchored end to end or that matches an arbitrary origin.

items.title: b.forms.validate anchors a field pattern to the whole submitted value
items.body: A field `pattern` is rendered verbatim as the HTML5 `pattern=` attribute, which the browser compiles anchored over the entire value. Server-side, `b.forms.validate` ran `pattern.test(value)` unanchored, so it accepted a value that only contained a match even though the browser rejects that value. An attacker bypassing the client (or any non-browser client) could submit `"12345"` against `pattern: /[0-9]{4}/`, or trailing payload past a short pattern, and pass server validation. Validation now matches the pattern against the whole value (`^(?:source)$`, preserving the `i`/`s`/`u` flags and dropping `g`/`y`/`m`), so the server and the browser agree. A pattern already written as `^...$` is unaffected.

items.title: b.middleware.cors refuses an unanchored or over-broad RegExp origin
items.body: Origin matching runs `pattern.test(origin)`, a substring match, and reflects a matched Origin into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. An unanchored pattern such as `/example\.com/` (a common "any subdomain" mistake) with `credentials:true` therefore reflected `https://example.com.attacker.test` and `https://myexample.com.evil.io`, a credentialed CORS bypass. `create()` previously screened RegExp origins for ReDoS only; it now also throws `cors/unanchored-pattern` for a pattern not anchored at both ends (`^...$`) and `cors/overbroad-pattern` for one that matches an arbitrary origin. Anchor RegExp origins so they match the complete origin, for example `/^https:\/\/([a-z0-9-]+\.)?example\.com$/`.
